title: What to eat in Darjeeling: momos to kinema
meta_description: A local guide to Darjeeling food: momos, thukpa, sel roti, gundruk, kinema, chhurpi, tongba and first-flush tea, with prices and where locals eat.
summary: Darjeeling's food is Nepali, Tibetan, Lepcha and Bhutia home cooking with a layer of old colonial bakery. Eat momos and thukpa where office workers eat them, try sel roti and aloo dum at a tea stall, look for gundruk, kinema and chhurpi, and drink first-flush tea without milk. A good day's food costs ₹400–800, indicative 2026.

sections.heading: The plate of the hills
paras: The food of Darjeeling follows its people. Nepali-speaking families, whose ancestors came from eastern Nepal to work the tea gardens, cook rice, dal, a seasonal vegetable, a pickle and, on good days, meat. Tibetan refugees, who came after 1959, brought noodle soups and dumplings that are now everyone's food. Lepcha and Bhutia families keep their own dishes and fermented drinks. Over all of it sits a British layer: bakeries, cream cakes, scones and the habit of afternoon tea.

Much of the hill diet is built on fermentation and drying, the old answer to long wet monsoons and cold winters when fresh vegetables were scarce. Leaves are fermented into gundruk, soybeans into kinema, radish into sinki, milk into chhurpi, and meat is dried over the kitchen fire. These flavours are sour, smoky and deep, and they are what makes a meal taste of the hills rather than of a hotel.
Chilli matters too. The local dalle khursani, a small round red chilli, is among the hottest in India. It turns up in pickles and chutneys on every table. Ask for less if you are not used to it.

paras: These are the dishes worth looking for, with indicative 2026 prices at ordinary eateries. Cafes on Chowrasta and the Mall charge more; the small places below Nehru Road and around Chowk Bazaar charge less.

sections.heading: Momos, noodles and Tibetan kitchens
paras: Momos are the food of Darjeeling now, eaten by everyone at every hour. A plate of eight to ten costs ₹60–150, served with a clear soup and a fierce red chilli sauce. Vegetable and paneer momos are cheapest; pork momos are the local favourite. Try them steamed first, then fried or in soup as jhol momo, swimming in a spiced tomato and sesame broth.

Noodle soups carry you through cold evenings. Thukpa is the familiar one, with round noodles; thenthuk uses flat, hand-pulled pieces and is more filling. In the Tibetan cafes of Gandhi Road, Dr Zakir Hussain Road and around Chowrasta, you will also find shapale, crisp fried bread filled with spiced meat; laphing, cold slippery mung-bean noodles in chilli, sold from street stalls; and butter tea, salty and rich, which many visitors find an acquired taste.

Wai Wai, a Nepali brand of instant noodles, deserves a mention because the hills love it. Kids eat it dry from the packet with chilli; stalls cook it as soup with egg. It costs ₹30–60 and is the snack most locals grew up on.

sections.heading: Nepali home food and the fermented flavours
paras: The heart of the hill diet is the daily dal-bhat: rice, lentils, a vegetable such as squash, mustard greens or the local iskus (chayote), and achar, a pickle of tomato, radish or chilli. Homestays serve it twice a day, and the simple eateries near the motor stands sell it as a thali for ₹120–300. It is the most filling, cheapest meal in town.

Look for the fermented foods. Gundruk is made from mustard, radish or cauliflower leaves, packed to ferment and then sun-dried; cooked as soup with soybeans and chilli it is sour and warming. Kinema is fermented soybean, sticky and strong, part of the Kirat tradition of the Limbu and Rai communities. Sinki is fermented radish. Chhurpi is cheese: the soft kind is crumbled into curries and chutneys, and the hard kind, dried in small blocks, is chewed for hours like a sweet.

Sel roti, a crisp ring of fried rice-flour batter, is made for festivals, above all Tihar in October or November, but tea stalls sell it every morning with aloo dum and milky tea. That breakfast costs under ₹100 and is the best start to a Darjeeling day.

sections.heading: Lepcha and Bhutia tables
paras: The Lepcha, who call themselves Rong and are the oldest inhabitants of these hills, have a food tradition rooted in the forest: wild ferns and greens, bamboo shoots, nettles, river fish and fermented millet. Their millet beer, chi, is traditionally drunk from bamboo vessels on social and ritual occasions. Lepcha food is mostly cooked at home, so the best chance to taste it is at a Lepcha homestay or during a community festival.

Bhutia and Sherpa kitchens share much with Tibet: dried meat, meat with radish, thick soups and butter tea. Across many hill communities you will meet tongba, a fermented millet drink served in a wooden or bamboo mug, topped up with hot water and sipped through a bamboo straw. It is mild, warming and social; ask in local eateries and homestays rather than tourist bars.

If you stay in a village homestay at Lepchajagat, Sittong or Chatakpur, ask the family to cook a local dish rather than the usual tourist menu. Many will happily make gundruk soup, a chicken curry with home-ground spices, squash shoots or nettle soup in season, often for no extra charge.

sections.heading: Bakeries, breakfasts and the old Mall menu
paras: The British left Darjeeling a taste for bakeries, and the town still has some of the best in the hills. Glenary's on Nehru Road, a bakery and restaurant in a building looking north over the valley, is the best known; its breakfasts, pastries and window seats are part of many family trips. Keventer's, also on Nehru Road, is known for its terrace breakfasts of sausages, ham and eggs. Expect to pay ₹300–700 a person for a full breakfast at the well-known names, indicative 2026.

Smaller bakeries around Chowrasta and Chowk Bazaar sell patties, cream rolls, cheese straws, fruit cake and fresh bread at local prices, ₹20–80 an item. In winter, hot chocolate and plum cake are part of the Christmas season, which Darjeeling's churches and schools celebrate warmly.

Bakeries are also the cheapest warm place to sit on a cold, wet afternoon. Order tea and a slice of cake for ₹80–150, find a window seat and watch the cloud move through the valley below. Many travellers remember that hour more than any sightseeing stop.

sections.heading: Tea, and how to eat well for less
paras: Tea is Darjeeling's own drink. In tea rooms near Chowrasta and on Nehru Road you can taste a named garden's first or second flush for ₹80–250 a cup. Drink it without milk and sugar to find the flavour. Ordinary roadside tea is a milky, sweet CTC blend from the plains at ₹10–20 a glass, and locals drink plenty of it too.
A few habits keep food costs low and the trip healthy:
list: Eat where office workers and drivers eat, in the lanes below Nehru Road and near Chowk Bazaar, not on Chowrasta.
Have breakfast at a tea stall instead of a ₹300 hotel breakfast.
Choose freshly steamed momos from busy places, where turnover is quick.
Carry a refillable bottle; hotels and many cafes fill it from filters.
Vegetarians eat well: veg momos, thukpa, dal-bhat, aloo dum and paneer dishes are everywhere, and many Marwari and Bengali eateries are pure vegetarian.
Go easy on dalle chilli and tongba on your first night, especially if you are going higher, such as to Sandakphu, the next day.

faqs.q: What is the famous food of Darjeeling
faqs.a: Momos and thukpa are what most visitors eat, but the true local foods are Nepali and Lepcha: dal-bhat with gundruk, kinema curry, sel roti with aloo dum, chhurpi cheese and the fiery dalle chilli pickle. Add first-flush Darjeeling tea, drunk without milk, and a bakery breakfast on Nehru Road, and you have tasted the town.

faqs.q: How much does a plate of momos cost in Darjeeling
faqs.a: About ₹60–150 for eight to ten pieces, indicative 2026, depending on filling and place. Vegetable momos are cheapest, pork and chicken cost more. Small eateries below Nehru Road and around Chowk Bazaar are cheaper than cafes on the Mall. Jhol momos, served in a spiced broth, cost a little more.

Gundruk is a fermented and sun-dried leafy green, made from mustard, radish or cauliflower leaves, and a staple of Nepali hill cooking. It is usually cooked as a sour soup with soybeans, tomatoes and chilli, or as a pickle. It was a way to keep greens through the winter, and it tastes tangy and earthy.

Kinema is fermented soybean, traditional among the Limbu and Rai communities of eastern Nepal, Darjeeling and Sikkim. Boiled soybeans are wrapped and left to ferment for a few days until sticky and strong-smelling, then cooked with onion, tomato and chilli as a curry. It is rich in protein and has a flavour some compare to Japanese natto.

Chhurpi is a hill cheese made from cow or yak milk. Soft chhurpi is crumbly, like cottage cheese, and is cooked in curries and chutneys. Hard chhurpi is pressed and dried into small, very hard blocks that people chew slowly for an hour or more. Packets of hard chhurpi are sold in shops and make good gifts.

Yes. Vegetable and paneer momos, veg thukpa, dal-bhat, aloo dum, sel roti and many curries are vegetarian, and the town has pure-vegetarian Marwari and Bengali eateries. Tell homestays in advance. Note that some soups and momo broths are made with meat stock, so ask if that matters to you.

Tongba is a drink of fermented millet, served in a tall wooden or bamboo mug. Hot water is poured over the grains, and you sip the warm, mildly alcoholic liquid through a bamboo straw, topping up with more water as you go. It belongs to the Limbu tradition and is drunk widely across the eastern Himalaya, especially in winter.

faqs.q: Where can I have breakfast with a view in Darjeeling
faqs.a: Glenary's on Nehru Road has window seats looking over the valley and is popular for breakfast and pastries. Keventer's, also on Nehru Road, is known for its terrace breakfasts. Expect ₹300–700 a person, indicative 2026. For a cheaper view, take tea and sel roti to a bench on Chowrasta at 7 am.

faqs.q: Is street food safe in Darjeeling
faqs.a: Generally yes, if you choose busy stalls where food is cooked fresh in front of you, such as momos straight from the steamer, hot aloo dum or tea. Avoid cut fruit and salads left out, and drink filtered or bottled water. Go easy on chilli on your first day. Most visitors eat on the street without trouble.
